A worker service exports the day's orders to a CSV file that a partner downloads every morning. Some days the file stops a few rows short, cut off mid-line. When the job retries, it fails with "The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process." Memory is fine, the CPU is idle and the logs show nothing else. The export method creates a
, writes the rows and returns. It never calls
, because the team assumed the garbage collector would close the file once the writer went out of scope.

is a memory optimization. It frees things a little sooner, but if you forget it, the garbage collector notices the object is gone and cleans up everything it held. In a managed language, you'd have to work hard to leak anything.
It's a reasonable conclusion. Most objects you create are never disposed and nothing bad happens, because all they hold is memory. Some disposable types really do have a fallback: a
that nobody disposes does close its file handle eventually. And in a quick test, a forgotten
rarely shows a symptom, because the process exits before anything runs out.
The trouble is the word "eventually". The GC was built to manage one resource, memory, and it decides when to run by looking at memory alone.
The GC frees memory, and only memory

Collections follow memory pressure, not handle pressure

The GC runs when allocations cross its thresholds or the machine runs low on memory. Running out of file handles or pooled connections triggers nothing, and an abandoned writer or connection is a tiny object, so a service with free memory can go a long time between collections while those resources stay taken. SqlClient's pool allows 100 connections by default; once all of them are checked out, the next

waits up to 15 seconds for one to come back, then fails with "Timeout expired. The timeout period elapsed prior to obtaining a connection from the pool." SqlClient can reclaim a connection nobody disposed, but only after the GC has collected the abandoned object. Under load, that's far too late.
Finalizers are a late safety net
Types that wrap a handle directly, usually through a

: a method the GC calls at some point after it finds the object unreachable. That's how the export's file is released in the end. But the exact time a finalizer runs is undefined, so is the thread it runs on, and since .NET 5, finalizers don't run at all when the process exits. Microsoft's guidance treats the finalizer as a safeguard for when
wasn't called, never as the plan.
